textbook: Clean cutaway textbook illustration of the ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM (ER) — a single continuous membrane ORGANELLE inside a eukaryotic cell, NOT a whole cell and NOT a bacterium — centred in a square 1:1 1080x1080 frame with generous negative space around it so labels can attach later. Fill the whole square edge-to-edge on a neutral dark-charcoal cytosol background with NO border, frame, vignette or letterbox. Match a refined educational plate: a MUTED, slightly desaturated palette (soft dusty tints, never bright primary or cartoon colours), THIN clean outlines (not heavy black strokes), gentle soft shading, each structure its own distinct soft colour fill. THE CENTRAL SUBJECT is the CONTRAST between two connected regions of ONE continuous membrane network, both clearly visible in the same frame: on one side (near a small patch of nuclear envelope at the frame's edge), draw ROUGH ER as 4-6 flattened, parallel, gently curved membrane sheets (cisternae) stacked close together in cool grey-blue (#9AA7B5), their OUTER (cytosolic) face densely and evenly stippled with many small dark warm-brown dots (#7A4438) — these are ribosomes, and they must be dense and regular, covering the sheets like fine stippling, never sparse. Between each pair of membrane lines leave a thin pale gap (#EAF1F5, the ER lumen). The sheets must be drawn CONNECTED to each other at their edges — never as separate isolated discs with gaps between them (that look belongs to the Golgi apparatus, a different organelle, and is the single most common mistake to avoid here). Follow the same membrane outward: the sheets should gradually narrow and open out into a branching, anastomosing mesh of rounded TUBULES in a lighter, slightly greener grey-blue (#B7C9C6) — this is SMOOTH ER — with the ribosome dots completely absent the moment the tubular region begins; the transition must read as one continuous membrane changing shape and losing its ribosomes, not two separate objects. Near the tubular smooth-ER region, add a small patch of soft sage green (#CFE0B8) where 2-3 small round mint-green (#7FC8A9) vesicle buds are shown pinching off the membrane — this is the transitional ER exit zone with transport vesicles heading away from the network. At the opposite edge from the smooth ER, show the rough-ER sheets merging directly, without any gap or break, into a short stretch of double-lined nuclear envelope (muted slate blue #6E7B8B) at the very corner of the frame — the ER must not float free of the nucleus. Optionally, small and clearly subordinate in a back corner, a tiny hint of a Golgi stack (desaturated amber-to-indigo gradient at low opacity) may sit near the transport vesicles, but it must stay small and not compete with the ER for attention. Fill remaining space with a neutral warm pale grey-beige cytosol (#EDE7DC), with a few isolated free ribosome dots scattered in it, not touching the membrane. CRITICAL SCIENTIFIC RULES: both rough ER (ribosome-studded sheets) and smooth ER (bare tubules) MUST appear together, connected, in one frame — an image with only one region fails. Ribosomes appear ONLY on the rough-ER sheets and briefly on the adjoining nuclear envelope patch, NEVER on the smooth-ER tubules. The rough-ER sheets must read as continuous and connected, never as separate sealed discs. Do NOT draw cristae (mitochondrial folds). Do NOT draw a bacterial nucleoid, cell wall, capsule, flagella or pili. Do NOT draw the ER as a closed bag or single sac. If a Golgi hint is included it must stay small and subordinate. Absolutely NO text, letters, numbers, labels, scale bars, arrows or watermarks in the image.
sem: Photorealistic false-color scanning electron micrograph / freeze-fracture SEM view of the ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM (ER) network inside a eukaryotic cell, fractured open to reveal both its sheet and tubule regions, centred in a square 1:1 1080x1080 frame with generous empty margin. Fill the whole square edge-to-edge with NO border, frame, vignette or letterbox. Subject: a fractured, three-dimensional membrane landscape whose surface reveals, in the same view, two distinct textures belonging to one continuous membrane. On one side, render a stack of flattened, gently curved parallel sheets (rough ER) in cool blue-grey false colour, their exposed cytosolic surfaces densely peppered with small, roughly round bumps (ribosomes) in a contrasting warm brown false colour — dense, even, unmistakable studding, never sparse. On the other side, the same membrane opens out and narrows into a branching network of smooth, rounded tubules (smooth ER) in a lighter, slightly greener-blue false colour, with a completely SMOOTH, bump-free surface — no ribosome texture anywhere on the tubules. The transition between the two textures should read as one continuous fractured membrane, not two separate objects touching. Near the tubular region, show 2-3 small round buds pinching away from the surface in a soft mint-green false colour (transport vesicles at a transitional-ER exit zone). At one edge of the frame, the sheet-stack should run into and fuse with a short stretch of double-layered nuclear envelope surface, itself lightly ribosome-studded, confirming the ER's origin at the nucleus. Shallow depth of field so the far background falls softly out of focus, cool studio microscopy lighting, crisp 3D surface relief typical of true freeze-fracture EM. CRITICAL: both the ribosome-studded sheet region and the bare tubular region MUST be visible together in one frame with a clear textural contrast between them — that contrast is the whole point of the image. Never put ribosome bumps on the tubular region. Do NOT show mitochondrial cristae, a bacterial cell wall/capsule/flagella, or a plant chloroplast. Do NOT draw the ER as a closed sac with no nuclear connection. Absolutely NO text, letters, numbers, labels, scale bars, arrows or watermarks anywhere in the image.
